</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Methodology</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Motivation</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we restrict our attention to linear transformations, i.e., <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>𝐖𝐱</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}</annotation></semantics></math>. Moreover, we will constrain our search space to orthogonal transformations, i.e., matrices <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math> that satisfy <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{T}=\mathbf{W}^{T}\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐖𝐖</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>𝐈</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{T}=\mathbf{W}^{T}\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{I}</annotation></semantics></math>. This is motivated by the universal geometry hypothesis – we expect cosine similarities to be preserved across embedding spaces. Later on, we will relax this assumption. Ultimately, the matrix will be the exponentially-smoothed average of a sequence of orthogonal matrices, enforcing orthogonality softly.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our linear approach addresses key limitations of existing methods: GANs are notoriously unstable and hard to train with many hyperparameters, require extensive computational resources and training time, and often need multiple seeds to achieve good solutions. In contrast, we know that in supervised cases (model stitching), there usually exists an affine mapping between latent spaces, suggesting the linear case is realizable – the question is how to find it efficiently. Our method requires significantly less data (60k vs. 1 million samples), runs on a CPU rather than requiring extensive GPU resources, and provides more stable training dynamics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Our method resembles <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hoshen and Wolf (2018)</a></cite>’s approach for word embeddings, proceeding in three main stages: approximate matching, transformation fitting, and iterative refinement. This scheme is very powerful, and we apply a similar method. We find that the approximate matching stage especially requires more delicate treatment in our case, so their approach is not applicable as-is.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The stages incrementally improve alignment quality – each stage builds upon structural correspondences to establish increasingly accurate alignments:</p>
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Approximate Matching:</span> Find approximate pairs of embeddings from both spaces using landmark points as anchors for relative representations</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Mapping Estimation:</span> Learn a linear orthogonal mapping from approximate matchings, where linearity and orthogonality provide an inductive bias to smooth out incorrect pairings</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Iterative Refinement:</span> Use the initial solution as a stepping stone for better matching/mapping, iterating until convergence or budget exhaustion</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.2" class="ltx_p">The overall process is described in Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ mini-vec2vec: Scaling Universal Geometry Alignment with Linear Transformations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Approximate Matching</h3>

<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Preprocessing.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first address arbitrary translations and scalings across embedding spaces. Both spaces are centered around their respective means and normalized to the unit hypersphere:</p>
<table id="S4.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.Ex2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\mu}_{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝝁</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\mu}_{A}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n_{A}}\mathbf{X}_{A}^{T}\mathbf{1}_{n_{A}},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_{A}=\mathbf{X}_{A}-\mathbf{1}_{n_{A}}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{A}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐗</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mn>𝟏</mn><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></msub></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐗</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐗</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mn>𝟏</mn><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝝁</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n_{A}}\mathbf{X}_{A}^{T}\mathbf{1}_{n_{A}},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_{A}=\mathbf{X}_{A}-\mathbf{1}_{n_{A}}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{A}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S4.Ex3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{A}[i,:]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐗</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>A</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mo rspace="0em">:</mo><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{A}[i,:]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex3.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_{A}[i,:]}{\|\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_{A}[i,:]\|_{2}},\quad\text{similarly for space }B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐗</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>A</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mo rspace="0em">:</mo><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐗</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>A</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mo rspace="0em">:</mo><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mo lspace="0em">∥</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mtext>similarly for space </mtext><mi>B</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_{A}[i,:]}{\|\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_{A}[i,:]\|_{2}},\quad\text{similarly for space }B</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\mu}_{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝝁</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\mu}_{A}</annotation></semantics></math> is the mean of space <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{1}_{n_{A}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mn>𝟏</mn><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{1}_{n_{A}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the vector of ones of length <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{A}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\|\cdot\|_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0em">∥</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em">∥</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\cdot\|_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the L2 norm.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Centroid Matching.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To establish structural correspondences, we employ an anchor discovery procedure based on multiple runs of clustering and matching. Each run consists of k-means clustering followed by solving a quadratic assignment problem (QAP) for cluster correspondence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In each run, we first perform k-means clustering on both embedding spaces independently to obtain cluster centroids <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathbf{c}^{A}_{j}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathbf{c}^{A}_{j}\}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathbf{c}^{B}_{j}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>B</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathbf{c}^{B}_{j}\}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j=1,\ldots,k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j=1,\ldots,k</annotation></semantics></math>. We then compute structural similarity matrices between cluster centroids:</p>
<table id="S4.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.Ex4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle S^{A}_{ij}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>A</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle S^{A}_{ij}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\cos(\mathbf{c}^{A}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{A}_{j}),\quad S^{B}_{ij}=\cos(\mathbf{c}^{B}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{B}_{j})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>B</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>B</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>B</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\cos(\mathbf{c}^{A}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{A}_{j}),\quad S^{B}_{ij}=\cos(\mathbf{c}^{B}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{B}_{j})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{c}^{A}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{c}^{A}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{c}^{B}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>B</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{c}^{B}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> are the <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th cluster centroids in spaces <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We find the optimal matching between cluster centroids by solving the quadratic assignment problem:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}^{*}=\operatorname{argmax}_{\mathbf{P}\in\Pi_{k}}\text{Tr}\left(\mathbf{S}_{A}^{T}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{S}_{B}\mathbf{P}^{T}\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐏</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>argmax</mi><mrow><mi>𝐏</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mtext>Tr</mtext></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐒</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐏𝐒</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}^{*}=\operatorname{argmax}_{\mathbf{P}\in\Pi_{k}}\text{Tr}\left(\mathbf{S}_{A}^{T}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{S}_{B}\mathbf{P}^{T}\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐏</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}</annotation></semantics></math> is a permutation matrix from the set <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Pi_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Pi_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> of all <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\times k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\times k</annotation></semantics></math> permutation matrices. For solving QAP, we use <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>-OPT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Croes, 1958</a>)</cite>. We run it 30 times and choose the permutation with the highest alignment score. This helps improve the robustness of the alignment over a single run of 2-OPT. Due to the small number of cluster centroids, this takes only a few seconds.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Relative Representations.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Once we have identified an alignment between centroids, we use the aligned centroids as anchors. For each run within the anchor discovery phase, we represent each embedding through its relationships to anchor points. For embedding <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}^{A}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}^{A}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> in a given run, we construct:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i}=[\cos(\mathbf{x}^{A}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{A}_{1}),\cos(\mathbf{x}^{A}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{A}_{2}),\ldots,\cos(\mathbf{x}^{A}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{A}_{k})]^{T}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i}=[\cos(\mathbf{x}^{A}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{A}_{1}),\cos(\mathbf{x}^{A}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{A}_{2}),\ldots,\cos(\mathbf{x}^{A}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{A}_{k})]^{T}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is the relative representation of the <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th embedding in space <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> with respect to the <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> cluster centroids from that run.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Robustification through Ensembling.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We improve robustness by concatenating relative representations from multiple runs:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i}=[\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i,1};\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i,2};\ldots;\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i,s}]\in\mathbb{R}^{sk}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo>;</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo>;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>;</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mi>A</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i}=[\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i,1};\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i,2};\ldots;\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i,s}]\in\mathbb{R}^{sk}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.2" class="ltx_p">This concatenation creates richer structural signatures that are more robust to clustering initialization randomness.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Anchor alignment algorithm is provided in Algorithm <a href="#alg2" title="Algorithm 2 ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ mini-vec2vec: Scaling Universal Geometry Alignment with Linear Transformations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Mapping Estimation</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We construct pseudo-parallel pairs by matching embeddings by similarity in relative space, averaging the <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> nearest neighbors to reduce noise:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex8.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{C}=\left\{\left(\mathbf{x}^{A}_{i},\frac{1}{k}\sum_{\mathbf{r}^{B}_{j}\in\mathcal{N}_{k}(\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i})}\mathbf{x}^{B}_{j}\right):i=1,\ldots,n_{A}\right\}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>k</mi></mfrac><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>B</mi></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></munder><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>B</mi></msubsup><mo rspace="0.278em">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}=\left\{\left(\mathbf{x}^{A}_{i},\frac{1}{k}\sum_{\mathbf{r}^{B}_{j}\in\mathcal{N}_{k}(\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i})}\mathbf{x}^{B}_{j}\right):i=1,\ldots,n_{A}\right\}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{N}_{k}(\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{N}_{k}(\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i})</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> nearest neighbors to <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> in the concatenated relative representation space. Note that the neighborhood information is obtained from the relative space (which is shared) and averaging takes place in the absolute space <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>. The orthogonal transformation is obtained via Procrustes analysis: <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}^{*}=\mathbf{V}\mathbf{U}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>𝐕𝐔</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}^{*}=\mathbf{V}\mathbf{U}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^{T}=\text{SVD}(\mathbf{A}^{T}\mathbf{B})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐔</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝚺</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐕</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>SVD</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐀</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐁</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^{T}=\text{SVD}(\mathbf{A}^{T}\mathbf{B})</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐀</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐁</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{B}</annotation></semantics></math> are matrices formed from the pseudo-parallel pairs in <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Iterative Refinement</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The initial transformation provides a coarse alignment that we refine with two complementary strategies. This refinement is crucial to improve alignment quality, with Refine-2 helping Refine-1 escape local minima. Pseudo-code is provided in Algorithms <a href="#alg3" title="Algorithm 3 ‣ 3 Problem Formulation ‣ mini-vec2vec: Scaling Universal Geometry Alignment with Linear Transformations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> &amp; <a href="#alg4" title="Algorithm 4 ‣ 3 Problem Formulation ‣ mini-vec2vec: Scaling Universal Geometry Alignment with Linear Transformations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Refine-1: Matching-based Refinement.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This refinement strategy proceeds by transforming embeddings from space <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> using <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math>, and averaging their nearest neighbors in space <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> based on cosine similarity, and obtaining a new orthogonal transformation with Procrustes analysis – similar to the process described in the Mapping Estimation stage (Section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Mapping Estimation ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ mini-vec2vec: Scaling Universal Geometry Alignment with Linear Transformations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>), with the crucial difference that now the similarity is performed in the ambient space <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> rather than relative space. The method is cheap and it runs for many iterations (50–100) using subsampling to boost computational efficiency.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We use exponential smoothing for transformation updates:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}^{(t+1)}=(1-\alpha)\mathbf{W}^{(t)}+\alpha\mathbf{W}_{\text{new}}^{(t)}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mtext>new</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}^{(t+1)}=(1-\alpha)\mathbf{W}^{(t)}+\alpha\mathbf{W}_{\text{new}}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">In the experiments below, we use <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0.5</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Refine-2: Clustering-based Refinement.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This strategy aims to improve the large-scale matching of embeddings by matching cluster centroids. We begin by clustering the embeddings in space <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math>. We then transform the <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> cluster centroids, and cluster the <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> embeddings <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">with the transformed <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> centroids as initialization</span>. The use of cluster centroids creates more stable pseudo-parallel pairs based on cluster assignments rather than individual nearest neighbors. The use of the transformed centroids as initialization follows from the assumption that they cannot be far off from cluster centroids in space <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>, so they will tend to converge to their counterpart centroids in space <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>, rather than arbitrary cluster centroids. This way, the seeded clustering will only correct minor errors in the transformation, and move the centroids to their “right positions” in space <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>. Similar to the first strategy, we use exponential smoothing.<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              Note that the above justification for Refine-2 is <span id="footnote2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">our</span> a priori rationale for using this method, and we do not make any claims as to whether this is the true reason for the ability of this method to improve the alignment. Our only claim is that we observe this step improves the alignment <span id="footnote2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">consistently</span>, and despite the fact that the Refine-1 <span id="footnote2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">has already converged and no longer shows improvement</span>.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Crucially, we find that <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">one</span> iteration of Refine-2 improves the alignment obtained by Refine-1. Curiously, two or more lead to a slight deterioration of the alignment, although this might be partly explained by our use of a number of clusters smaller than the dimensionality.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We replicate the in-distribution experiment from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jha et al. (2025)</a></cite>. We run the algorithm for all pairs among the 5 sets of text encoders used in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jha et al. (2025)</a></cite>. The encoders are summarized in Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Analysis. ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ mini-vec2vec: Scaling Universal Geometry Alignment with Linear Transformations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. Experiments use k-means clustering from scikit-learn <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pedregosa et al., 2011</a>)</cite>, QAP is solved with the scipy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Virtanen et al., 2020</a>)</cite> implementation of 2-OPT.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We take a random subset of the Natural Questions dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwiatkowski et al., 2019</a>)</cite> of size <math id="S5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="60,000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>60,000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">60,000</annotation></semantics></math> and compute sentence embeddings under all possible encoders. We leave <math id="S5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8192" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8192</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8192</annotation></semantics></math> sentences for evaluation. For each pair, we split the remaining embeddings equally between the source encoder (space <math id="S5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math>) and target encoder (space <math id="S5.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>), so there is no overlap between the source and target sentences. All experiments are run on a Colab notebook with a CPU runtime, and repeated three times for each pair to demonstrate consistency. We compare the results to the numbers reported in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jha et al. (2025)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Metrics.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate alignment quality using two primary metrics. The first is <span id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Top-1 Accuracy</span>, the fraction of queries where the nearest neighbor in the target space is the correct match, defined by</p>
<table id="S5.Ex10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.Ex10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Accuracy}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\delta(\text{NN}(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{a}_{i})=\mathbf{b}_{i})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>Accuracy</mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext>NN</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐖𝐚</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝐛</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Accuracy}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\delta(\text{NN}(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{a}_{i})=\mathbf{b}_{i}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta</annotation></semantics></math> is the indicator function, <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{NN}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>NN</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{NN}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is the nearest neighbor of source embedding <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> in the target space, and <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{b}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐛</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{b}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is its true corresponding target embedding. The second is the <span id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Average Rank</span>, the mean position of the true match in the sorted list of distances from the query to all targets,</p>
<table id="S5.Ex11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.Ex11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{AvgRank}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\text{rank}(\mathbf{b}_{i}|\mathbf{a}_{i})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>AvgRank</mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><mrow><mtext>rank</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐛</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{AvgRank}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\text{rank}(\mathbf{b}_{i}|\mathbf{a}_{i}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">We also report the mean <span id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">cosine similarity</span> after each step of the algorithm to show its progression over the stages. Cosine similarity in itself can be used as an evaluation metric, but it can also be misleading. Cosine similarity in <span id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mini-vec2vec</span> underestimates the similarity in the original space, due to the removal of the mean vector, which is a dominant part of all vectors, accounting for <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim 30\%-70\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>70</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim 30\%-70\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the vector’s norm. Also, setups that move the vectors to a third space, like <span id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span>, have an advantage as they can change the geometry. Our setup does not change the geometry.<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            Apart from translation and scaling, which, formally speaking, are a form of transition to a third space, but in a very restricted sense.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Hyperparameters.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We have found that the method is extremely robust to hyperparameter choices, as long as they are in a reasonable range. We use <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s=30" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s=30</annotation></semantics></math> runs of relative representation alignment with <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c=20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c=20</annotation></semantics></math> clusters. We use <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=50</annotation></semantics></math> neighbors in Mapping Estimation. We set the sampling rate in Refine-1 to <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{s}=10,000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>10,000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{s}=10,000</annotation></semantics></math> and utilize <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k^{\prime}=50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>k</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k^{\prime}=50</annotation></semantics></math> neighbors; In Refine-2, we use <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c^{\prime}=500" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>500</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c^{\prime}=500</annotation></semantics></math> clusters. For exponential smoothing, we use <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0.5</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Note this is a rather economical choice of hyperparameters, which we would not suggest using a priori. It turned out to work well, regardless. The full hyperparameter configuration used in the experiments is also documented in the code linked. For the <span id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">gtr</span>-<span id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">gte</span> pair, we increase the number of clusters to <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c=30" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c=30</annotation></semantics></math>. We find that for this pair, the algorithm often converges to a sub-optimal solution in the <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c=20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c=20</annotation></semantics></math> regime.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Results.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3 Problem Formulation ‣ mini-vec2vec: Scaling Universal Geometry Alignment with Linear Transformations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, we demonstrate that our approach matches or exceeds <span id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> across (almost) the entire table. The improvement is more noticeable in the rank metric. Importantly, the method is extremely robust, as is evidenced by the small standard deviation, already by the end of the first refinement step. Unlike <span id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span>, our method does not collapse on the <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e5</annotation></semantics></math>-<math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="gtr" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">gtr</annotation></semantics></math> pair or the <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="gtr" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">gtr</annotation></semantics></math>-<math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="gte" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">gte</annotation></semantics></math> pair.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We underline scores that are within a <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.01</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.01</annotation></semantics></math> margin, as they might result from rounding noise and stochasticity, and a slightly different experimental setup.<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">4</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            Our results are calculated over multiple runs and a single evaluation set, while vec2vec computes the results of a single run over 8 evaluation sets.</span></span></span> Due to the small variance in most experiments, in both methods, we believe that a <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.01</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.01</annotation></semantics></math> margin is a good compromise. The superior results are an additional benefit, but even where the results are not superior, but rather matching performance, it is achieved for a fraction of the cost. Moreover, even where <span id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> collapses, we observe <span id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mini-vec2vec</span> still reaches good performance. Computationally, one run of <span id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mini-vec2vec</span> is completed on a CPU in less than ten minutes, while <span id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> requires 1–7 days on a GPU, depending on the hardware.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Analysis.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We observe that despite variation in the approximate matching phase (Initial), Refine-1 consistently improves cosine similarity and converges to stationary points with nearly identical cosine similarity values across different random initializations. This reproducible convergence behavior suggests the optimization landscape is well-structured.
The convergence of Refine-1 appears to reach a stationary point of the implicit nearest-neighbor matching objective. However, applying Refine-2 successfully improves upon this converged solution. The two algorithms appear to optimize different implicit proxy objectives, and both contribute to reaching a good solution.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T2" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S5.T2.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">

<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Discussion</h2>

<section id="S6.SSx1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">Choice of Hyperparameters</h3>

<div id="S6.SSx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The <span id="S6.SSx1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mini-vec2vec</span> algorithm is reasonably stable under different choices of parameters, often converging to similar stationary points. Moreover, unlike many machine learning algorithms, most hyperparameters have a clear interpretation and frequently have a monotone behavior. For example, generally speaking, increasing the following hyperparameters should improve the outcome (or at least not harm). Importantly, while <span id="S6.SSx1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">some</span> of these trends have been observed empirically in some setups, a full experimental analysis has not been made, and so the explanations below on how to choose hyperparameters are suggestions at best, and <span id="S6.SSx1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">should not be trusted blindly</span>.</p>
<ul id="S6.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S6.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Number of concatenated representations</span>: The more concatenated alignments we use, the more likely it is for noisy assignments to be diluted, emphasizing the signal from true assignments. Note that this helps stabilize the algorithm, meaning it is less likely to meet failure modes in the average and worst cases. However, even with fewer alignments, good alignments can be reached, but the probability of failure modes might increase.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Number of iterations</span>: We find that the alignment is monotonically increasing as the number of iterations grows. This makes it a safe bet to increase the number of iterations if one is unsure whether convergence has been reached. Across all cases examined, we found convergence to be quite fast. Almost without exception, 100 iterations were more than enough, by a large margin.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Subsampling rate</span>: Subsampling allows us to speed up the algorithm quite substantially, but it can increase noise. The larger the sample size is, the closer this approximation is to the data. We generally consider higher sampling rates to be better.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S6.SSx1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SSx1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Other hyperparameters are less obvious. <span id="S6.SSx1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Number of clusters</span> in the approximate matching step is likely good in moderation. While it gives us more landmark points for alignment, it can theoretically lead to instabilities, because the assignment of very granular centroids can be noisy. Increasing <span id="S6.SSx1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">number of neighbors</span> is often beneficial, to a point. It helps reduce noise, as averaging more neighbors leads to a smoother estimate of the true aligned position. Note that this is in contrast to multilingual word embeddings, where essentially every point has a ground-truth translation, and it makes sense to rely on a single neighbor. Increasing the number of neighbors to very large numbers might lead to over-smoothing, which may harm performance eventually.
Finally, increasing the exponential smoothing parameter <math id="S6.SSx1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> leads to higher cosine scores, but they don’t necessarily translate to better rank and top-1 scores. This is likely due to overfitting. The smoothing parameter is implicitly responsible for the maximum distance of the matrix from being orthogonal. While this (alleged) overfitting phenomenon has been observed by us empirically, we did not explore it rigorously, and it might not be a common case. Additionally, increasing <math id="S6.SSx1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> makes convergence slightly slower.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SSx1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SSx1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Unlike many deep learning setups – GANs in particular – the range of hyperparameters that lead to strong performance is generously wide. Each hyperparameter is interpretable, and one can plausibly guess in which direction to modify the parameter in order to improve effectiveness, if needed.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SSx2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">Failure Modes</h3>

<div id="S6.SSx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SSx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We find that despite the many experiments we ran, including ones with different configurations, failure modes were extremely rare. In fact, we didn’t experience <span id="S6.SSx2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">any</span> failure modes except with the <span id="S6.SSx2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">gte</span> model. Moreover, all failure modes were around the <span id="S6.SSx2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">gte-gtr</span> pair, and modifying the number of clusters to <math id="S6.SSx2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c=30" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c=30</annotation></semantics></math> solved this, though experimentation with more runs has shown that failure modes still exist in <span id="S6.SSx2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">gtr</span> <math id="S6.SSx2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="S6.SSx2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">gte</span> – they are just rarer. Crucially, failure modes are <span id="S6.SSx2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">not</span> catastrophic. The failure modes are characterized by worse top-1 accuracy and average rank (and slightly lower cosine similarity throughout the refinement steps. Often also noticeable in the initial step, but not always). But the decrease is not catastrophic, leading to <math id="S6.SSx2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim 90\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim 90\%</annotation></semantics></math> top-1 accuracy and <math id="S6.SSx2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5-10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5-10</annotation></semantics></math> average rank, much better than any naive baseline.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The study of universality has its roots in several works. Representation alignment is well-studied in the supervised setup. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lenc and Vedaldi (2015)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bansal et al. (2021)</a></cite> demonstrated that linear transformations are often sufficient for aligning neural network representations through their <span id="S7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">stitching</span> approach. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Olah (2015)</a></cite> studied the equivalence of neural networks in relative terms. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Moschella et al. (2023)</a></cite> have used these insights to encode a universal space where data points are represented relative to anchor points, utilizing it for zero-shot stitching. Similarly, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dar et al. (2023)</a></cite> have demonstrated zero-shot stitching using a method equivalent to relative representations with token embeddings as anchors.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huh et al. (2024)</a></cite> have aggregated and unified previous work, under the name <span id="S7.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Platonic Representation Hypothesis</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The task of unsupervised alignment of embeddings has a long history in word embeddings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Conneau et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen and Cardie, 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grave et al., 2018</a>)</cite> and machine translation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lample et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Artetxe et al., 2018</a>)</cite>. Most of the works rely on training a GAN. They often require a small seed of matched pairs in order to work. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hoshen and Wolf (2018)</a></cite> avoid the adversarial setup and use a three-step algorithm similar to ours. Their approach, specifically their approximate matching process, which relied on PCA, was insufficient for our purposes.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">8 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We have presented <span id="S8.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mini-vec2vec</span>, a linear approach to unsupervised embedding alignment that achieves competitive performance while offering substantial advantages in computational efficiency, training stability, and interpretability. Our method demonstrates that adversarial training may be unnecessary for reliable embedding alignment, provided that structural correspondences can be estimated accurately.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The success of our approach provides strong empirical evidence for the universal geometry hypothesis and suggests that the geometric regularities in learned representations are more robust and accessible than previously assumed. By decomposing the alignment problem into classical optimization components, we achieve both theoretical clarity and practical efficiency.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The efficiency and accessibility of our method could democratize research on embedding alignment and cross-modal representation learning. By reducing computational barriers, we enable broader participation in this research area and facilitate deployment in resource-constrained environments. From a security perspective, efficient alignment methods raise important considerations about data privacy and intellectual property protection in embedding spaces. If alignment can be performed quickly and reliably, it may become easier to leak data in the scenario described in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jha et al. (2025)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">

    <p>We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile
      support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the
      methods listed below:</p>
    <ul>
      <li>Click the "Report Issue" <span class="mobile-only">(<svg role="presentation"
            style="display: inline-block; vertical-align: middle; fill: var(--text-color);" aria-hidden="true"
            height="1em" viewBox="0 0 640 640">

          </svg>)</span> button, located in the page header.</li>
    </ul>
    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
    <p>Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a
        class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML"
        target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a class="ltx_ref"
        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
